claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite has direct tungsten–copper interfaces and no surface modification on the tungsten particles.
Applying a uniform nanometer-thick graphene coating to tungsten particles before embedding them in copper creates interfacial graphene layers at the W–Cu boundary.
Graphene has exceptionally high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Graphene can form strong van der Waals bonds at metal interfaces.
An interfacial graphene layer at the W–Cu boundary reduces interfacial thermal resistance.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance facilitates more efficient phonon transport across the W–Cu interface.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance facilitates more efficient electron transport across the W–Cu interface.
Graphene-coated tungsten particles significantly increase the overall thermal conductivity of a W–Cu composite relative to an otherwise comparable uncoated composite.
The graphene coating does not degrade the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
The graphene coating does not degrade the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
The proposed benefit should hold in high-temperature, moderate-irradiation environments typical of heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
The thermal-conductivity benefit depends on the graphene coating remaining intact and stable during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Degradation or delamination of the graphene layer would limit the proposed thermal-transport mechanism.
